introHtml:
If you're searching for mobile home tie down replacement in Ocala, it's usually because someone else forced the issue. Your insurance company sent a letter asking for tie-down certification, a lender flagged the anchors during financing, or an inspector crawled under the home before closing and found rusted straps. We handle all of it: replacing corroded or loose straps, adding frame and longitudinal anchors, and issuing the certification paperwork that gets insurers and underwriters off your back.

Marion County sits in Florida Wind Zone II, which means your home needs a specific number of properly rated anchors and straps, not just whatever was installed in 1985. Most full anchoring packages here run $1,500 to $3,000, and a standalone certification inspection is $150 to $300. Call (352) 247-3105 and we'll give you a free written estimate, and if the home also needs work underneath, we can bundle it with mobile home leveling in the same visit.

sections.heading: Why Insurance Companies Are Demanding Tie-Down Certifications
sections.html:
Over the past few years, Florida insurers have gotten strict about manufactured home anchoring. Many carriers now require a current tie-down certification letter before they'll write or renew a policy, and some send non-renewal notices that give homeowners 30 to 45 days to produce one. It's frustrating, but from the insurer's side it makes sense: a properly anchored home is far less likely to shift or overturn in a storm, and they price risk accordingly.

The certification itself is straightforward. We crawl the full length of the home, count and inspect every anchor and strap, check tension and corrosion, and compare what's there against the Wind Zone II standard for your home's size. If the system passes, you get a signed letter, usually the same week, for $150 to $300.

If it doesn't pass, you get an itemized list of exactly what's missing or failed, with pricing to fix it. Most correction jobs land between $1,500 and $3,000, and once the work is done we issue the certification at no extra inspection charge. One call, one crew, paperwork handled.

sections.heading: Wind Zone II Requirements for Ocala and Marion County
sections.html:
All of Marion County, along with Sumter and Citrus counties, falls in Florida Wind Zone II. That zone sets the minimum anchoring standard: homes must be secured with ground anchors and straps rated for higher wind loads than Zone I homes, spaced closer together, and include both frame ties and longitudinal stabilization. A pre-1994 home that was fine under the old rules often falls short of what today's inspectors and insurers look for.

Here's what a compliant Wind Zone II system generally includes:

  • Ground anchors driven to proper depth for our sandy Central Florida soil, with stabilizer plates where required
  • Frame straps connecting the steel chassis to each anchor at the required spacing
  • Longitudinal anchors resisting end-to-end movement, typically at the corners and along the centerline
  • Proper tension on every strap, since a loose strap does almost nothing in a storm

We serve the whole area, including Silver Springs, Belleview, Summerfield, Dunnellon, Lady Lake, and Citra.

sections.heading: Selling or Financing a Mobile Home? Get the Certification First
sections.html:
Tie-down certifications come up at two moments in a sale: when the buyer's lender orders one as a condition of financing, and when the buyer's insurance company requires one to bind coverage. Either way, if the paperwork isn't ready, the closing date slips. We've seen deals stall for weeks over a $150 to $300 inspection that takes us about an hour on site.

If you're the seller, getting certified before you list is the smart move. You'll know about any anchor problems while you still have time to fix them on your schedule, instead of negotiating repairs under deadline pressure with a buyer holding the leverage. A current certification letter also gives buyers one less reason to hesitate.

If you're mid-transaction and the clock is running, call the 24/7 line at (352) 247-3105. We prioritize pre-closing inspections and can usually get under the home within a day or two. While we're down there, we'll also flag anything else an inspector would catch, like a torn vapor barrier or settling piers, so there are no surprises at the four-point inspection.

sections.heading: How Tie-Down Replacement Works and What It Costs
sections.html:
Every job starts with a free written estimate. We inspect the existing system, count what's salvageable, and quote the exact number of anchors and straps needed to bring the home to Wind Zone II standard. No vague allowances, just line items you can check against the finished work.

On installation day, the crew removes failed straps, drives new ground anchors to depth, installs frame and longitudinal ties, and tensions everything to spec. Most single-wide homes are done in a day; double-wides usually take one to two days. Full packages run $1,500 to $3,000, with smaller repair jobs, like replacing a handful of corroded straps, costing less.

Anchoring works best on a level home, since an out-of-level frame puts uneven load on straps and loosens them over time. If your doors stick or floors slope, it's worth checking what leveling costs and handling both in one visit. We can also reinstall or replace skirting after the work so the home looks finished, not worked on.

faq.q: How much is a tie-down certification inspection?
faq.a: A certification inspection costs $150 to $300. We inspect every anchor and strap under the home, check tension and corrosion, and compare the system to Florida Wind Zone II requirements. If it passes, you get a signed certification letter, usually within the same week.

We can usually inspect within a day or two, and if the system passes, the letter follows quickly. If repairs are needed, most correction jobs finish in one to two days, and we issue the certification as soon as the work is complete.

faq.q: What does Wind Zone II require for my mobile home?
faq.a: Marion, Sumter, and Citrus counties are all in Florida Wind Zone II. That means your home needs ground anchors and straps rated for higher wind loads, spaced closer together than Zone I, plus frame ties and longitudinal anchors to resist end-to-end movement. Older homes, especially pre-1994 installs, often come up short on longitudinal anchors, and that's the most common fix we make.

faq.q: How do I know if my tie-down straps need replacing?
faq.a: The common failure signs are visible rust or flaking on the straps, slack you can move by hand, anchors that have pulled up or tilted in the soil, and straps that have snapped outright. Florida humidity and our sandy soil accelerate all of these. If your home is more than 15 to 20 years old and the straps have never been checked, a $150 to $300 inspection will tell you exactly where things stand.
